title: AI Product Photography: A Practical Guide | AIVideosUGC
description: AI product photography: turn one photo into images for a product page and social posts, with no photo shoot. See what to upload and how to choose the setting.
h1: AI Product Photography: Getting Usable Shots From One Photo
lead: One clear photo can become a new setting, a white catalog image, or the item on a person. Compare every result with what you actually ship.
summary: A sharp photo turns into a new setting, a white catalog image, or the item on a person. Compare it with the product you ship.

sections.h2: A New Place for the Same Item
paras: The same item can sit in new light without a second shoot. Put the soy candle on the wood table you already use for the shop photos, and ask for late-afternoon light through a window. If the candle's shape changes, throw that file out.
Begin with one sharp photo. Name the surface and the light, then compare the result with the item you ship. Open the [photo tools](page:photo-hub) once the source photo is sharp.
sections.alt: A hand sets tan handbag beside a folded scarf on an entry table.

sections.h2: Why Shops Switch to AI Product Photos
paras: Lower spend. A product photo is 24 credits, and [plans start on the pricing page](page:pricing). You pay credits per image instead of booking a studio for every new scene.
Less waiting. You skip the back-and-forth of hiring a photographer. The next scene does not wait on their calendar.
Several shots from one file. Make the product-page image, a social scene, and a close view from the same upload. Each of those is its own image.
No model to book. Stage the product with a single extra object. When someone should wear it, use [model photos](page:model-photos) instead of hiring a model.
The person who packs orders at night can still make the next tea tin scene after the bench is clear.
A second scene to compare. Render another background from the same photo and keep the one that fits the post. The product in the frame should stay the product you ship.

sections.h2: How to Generate an AI Product Image in 3 Steps
paras: A phone picture of the olive oil beside a window is enough. If you would rather not upload yet, write one sentence about a wood table and afternoon light.
For the oil, ask for the bottle standing alone on white if the page needs a hero. Ask for a hand pouring it only when you want a use shot. Describe the look in plain words.
When the bottle looks right, download the square file. If the label letters melted, write a shorter note and run it again. That still can later be the first frame of a clip.

paras: You can ask for a kitchen, a window, or the item alone on white. A cutting board, a rainy windowsill, and a kettle on white are enough to see the range.

For the first marketplace image, make [white background product photos](page:white-background) from the same photo. Use the [background changer](page:change-background) when only the backdrop should change, or [lifestyle photos](page:lifestyle-photos) when the product should sit in a room.

The same upload often does more than one job.
A beauty shop keeps the jar large in every frame, then sets that still beside the real product on the shelf.
Someone who has never opened a photo editor can still make the next scene for a wool beanie, as long as the photo shows the real beanie.
A gadget shop approves the still of the charger first. Only then does it ask for a clip where a hand holds that same charger.
A jewelry shop changes the on-screen price in the same project as the necklace photo, so the caption matches today's tag.
A supplements brand keeps the tub on the same counter and records a second line for the country it ships to next.
A small team makes the next set of stills on a monthly plan instead of booking another half day.
A clothing shop builds launch photos from garment pictures and talks about the garment.
A food brand shoots one pack photo per flavor in daylight, then asks for a new table only when that pack is the one in the box.
A store owner who usually writes the caption by hand can still get a square still and stop there. No second screen is required for that photo.
A clip can start from the product page once the tote photo is the one you ship. Read the spoken line before anyone posts it.

One photo can cover the product page and a paid post, without a second shoot. The sneaker picture you took for the box can do both of those jobs. The shoe in the file still has to match the shoe you ship.

A new product page wants more than one picture. A seasonal post wants a new setting. A supplier photo may not match the rest of the store. When a buyer must see stitching or the ports on a charger, a close-up you photographed is still the safer file.

paras: A marketplace hero and a social post can come from the same photo, once you pick the destination. A marketplace hero has stricter rules than a social post.

A first image usually wants a clean white field and nothing extra in the frame. Later photos can show use, scale, or a detail. On your own store, match the backdrop you already use so the row stays tidy. Product photos come out square, which fits a product page and a social crop.

sections.h2: How Do I Check a Photo Before I Publish It?
paras: Put the image beside the product in your hand. Compare color, shape, the size of each part, logos, and how many pieces there are.

Zoom in on labels, buttons, and edges. If something is wrong, render again from a sharper photo or a clearer sentence instead of hiding it with a caption. Use your own label and your own logo. The [Content Policy](/content) says what can be uploaded. Uploads and results stay in your account and are not shown publicly.
sections.alt: Hands inspect tan handbag beside a blank phone.

paras: One daylight photo and a plain sentence are enough for the next scene. Compare the result with the real item before it goes on a product page.
White images and room scenes are separate jobs. A finished image can run in ads and on your store, and it does not carry a watermark.

faq.q: What can an AI product photo tool create?
faq.a: It makes a store photo from a picture you already have: a new setting, a white field, or the item on a person. Product photos come out square. You still compare the photo with the item you ship.

faq.q: How does the photo get made?
faq.a: Upload a sharp photo. Say you want it on a wood table, not on marble. If a job fails, those credits come back.

faq.q: What should I look for in the tool?
faq.a: A photo that still looks like your product, and a setting you can name. AIVideosUGC is built for that shop task.

faq.q: Do I need a paid plan to make product photos?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits. You see the cost of each image before it runs.

faq.q: Is this a fit for an online store?
faq.a: Yes. A marketplace hero and a paid still can both come from it. When a buyer must see the stitching or the ports, photograph that close-up yourself.

faq.q: What do I get from it?
faq.a: New settings without a studio booking, more than one scene from the same photo, someone wearing the item without a hired model, and a second version when you want to test a background.

faq.q: Can I use the photo on my store and in ads?
faq.a: Yes. A finished image can run in ads and on your store. It has no watermark. Compare it with the item you ship before you publish. The [Content Policy](/content) covers what you can upload.

faq.q: What if the product in the result looks different?
faq.a: Render it again from a sharper photo or a clearer sentence.
